author: Lorddo [ALRT]
content: Hey @Lorddo , you did some nice calculations here! Thank you for sharing this.   We did very similar calculations and I want to share them with you. We calculated the average burn rates for the different ship sizes and looked at the ships that are staked in SCORE, not the total supply of all ships. And we even further reduced the number of ships staked in SCORE with the fleets that are no longer refilled -> inactive fleets. So our numbers are different, but of course it's still a shortage in production. If you take ammo for example, your supply/demand ratio is 0.176. In our calculation we see this ratio at 0.505. Of course we know, they're likely to change the number of supply here and there are other assumptions that we've made. For example, the claim stakes may not sell out and therefore the supply of R4s will be even less. Anyway, I like the fact that you are doing these calculations and sharing them, so I wanted to reply.

author: defiantwyvern
content: Bear in mind, we are driving heavily towards a player driven economy. Earnings potential is not exclusive to ATLAS emissions through the inflation curve. Players will be freely trading value with one another for specific specializations. For example, extraction and crafting being sold p2p. Not everyone will want to do that, so they'll have to purchase from another player. Also, a large fleet owner employing other players from around the world to operate their assets and paying a wage. This does not come from the emission curve. The only way we reach sustainable economy is by enabling and encouraging the exchange of value between users.

This reminds me a lot of Star Citizen in the early days, when Elite Dangerous was being introduced  Of course Chris said that more games in the space X4 genre would only bring more interest to the genre & theme, which would be a net win as many might next look at Star Citizen, given that most people buy & play multiple games per year.

If Star Atlas was a similar sort of legacy game, then you would not doubt get a similar answer, as admitting you feel threatened would spread and show weakness, likely deterring people from looking much further   You never get an honest answer, as that leads to PR nightmares.

However, Star Atlas being the first game of such scope being made available running on the blockchain, using blockchain assets makes this a whole other ballgame. That is such a huge differentiator that I can now finally say that Chris his answer back in the day would indeed be applicable here.

If people play Starfield and like it, and are looking for an MMO that has some overlap in the space genre, then Star Atlas would be an obvious way to go due to the benefits it will provide over those legacy games  That is.. once gamers stop being allergic to NFTs of course

content: This would be presuming ATLAS/POLIS would be liquid if people feel an imminent implosion. Time and time again in crypto markets it's been demonstrated that everyone cashes out on a sinking ship and assets quickly trend to 0. author: MrTixlUstur
content:
Unlike stocks and bonds, crypto escapes one rule that applies solely to financial securities:  the “wash sale” rule.*  Securities are regulated financial instruments with rules to protect investors. Since cryptocurrency is largely unregulated, it isn’t a “security” so the wash sale rule does not apply.  This means crypto has the same trading rules as precious metals including gold and silver or “real” currencies such as the British pound or Euro.

Cryptocurrency is volatile and prices change rapidly. Because you can ignore the wash sale rule, you can sell coins / NFTs during market declines to reduce losses and then quickly buy back those coins / NFTs as prices bottom out. You can apply those losses against other capital gains to lower their overall taxable profit. In years where these losses are substantial, they can be carried forward to offset future gains.

It is important to note that this may be a temporary tax loophole. The rules may change as a result of pending legislation.

By Jon C. Holmes, CPA, LSWG Managing Principal

author: Signal
content: Unlike stocks and bonds, crypto escapes one rule that applies solely to financial securities:  the “wash sale” rule.*  Securities are regulated financial instruments with rules to protect investors. Since cryptocurrency is largely unregulated, it isn’t a “security” so the wash sale rule does not apply.  This means crypto has the same trading rules as precious metals including gold and silver or “real” currencies such as the British pound or Euro.  Cryptocurrency is volatile and prices change rapidly. Because you can ignore the wash sale rule, you can sell coins / NFTs during market declines to reduce losses and then quickly buy back those coins / NFTs as prices bottom out. You can apply those losses against other capital gains to lower their overall taxable profit. In years where these losses are substantial, they can be carried forward to offset future gains.  It is important to note that this may be a temporary tax loophole. The rules may change as a result of pending legislation.  By Jon C. Holmes, CPA, LSWG Managing Principal

author: [AEP] Mendizo
content: Yes. Our Player Profile system is designed specifically to manage permissions and authority of user accounts. With this system, it would be entirely possible for a person to provide access to ships and define any number of parameters restricting behavior. For example, the Player Profile could enable someone to borrow an asset for a fixed period of time, for a fixed cost (or free, if you want your guild mates to use it), while limiting the ability for them to move the asset out of the account, sell it, or engage in HRZ combat.

author: Lorddo [ALRT]
content: Yes. Our Player Profile system is designed specifically to manage permissions and authority of user accounts. With this system, it would be entirely possible for a person to provide access to ships and define any number of parameters restricting behavior. For example, the Player Profile could enable someone to borrow an asset for a fixed period of time, for a fixed cost (or free, if you want your guild mates to use it), while limiting the ability for them to move the asset out of the account, sell it, or engage in HRZ combat.

author: [AEP] Steve WoodyMUD
content: I don't take issue with bots in the marketplace. Generally I think they're positive for liquidity and price discovery. I appreciate it can be a little frustrating being outpriced (up or down) by a penny because it can be automated by a bot, but bot accounts are also getting tagged, or at least recognized by human accounts and players.  The game is going to be largely different. Given sufficiently complex gameplay mechanics, a lot of processes, or at least advanced gameplay will not be prone to automation. Plus, there are real risks operating within Star Atlas and SAGE, disincentivizing the use of bots. Just too much uncertainty in gameplay. And we'll also be building in certain gamified captchas in the game that require human interaction.   With that said, I'd also point to our development methodology to better understand our philosophy. We are building on-chain game logic with intention. 6+ on-chain programs being deployed for SAGE. This is complex, and wouldn't make sense, with the exception of the fact that it opens up our entire platform to permissionless development. The Club is probably the best example I can provide at the moment, but they built a program that helps players restock ships of R4 resources. It interacts directly with our Faction Fleet program. They didn't ask us to do it, and don't need to. That tool is a simple demonstration of the type of third party services that will be built on top of the SA ecosystem. It benefits the developers should they choose to monetize, it benefits the players with additional features, and it benefits us in that we get more people building, at no cost, and arguably a better experience for our players. It's at the core of what we do. Will be interesting to see where it all goes with the third party services, and we certainly don't want a feature in place that diminishes the experience for everyone else, but I fully encourage this type of innovation.  Prospective benefit of on-chain development, although much longer term, is the idea of censorship resistance. If we can ever get to a point where game servers are decentralized, and much of the logic exists on the blockchain (Solana), Star Atlas as a game and a metaverse essentially replicate what only bitcoin has been able to do in terms of decentralization and censorship resistance. It couldn't ever be stopped.

author: SW4GN3R [STAR]
content:
Also, on the economics side, I'd like to emphasize that while the emission curve is in place to bootstrap the economy and provide the initial income value for players, long term I believe value will exist on a P2P basis. Trading resources, selling loot, lending out assets, providing services and conveniences in game, etc. For example, someone might make a living operating their rescue ship getting paid by players that need the assistance. Or someone operating a taxi/Uber service on a CSS with their Lowbies. Or taking the Bitboat out for tours of the universe.

The future of this virtual world will rely on people coming in and spending money - not just on those that are looking to withdraw value from it. Which is why I think the CSS's will be really attractive with their commercial centers. When mainstream real world brands set up shop and sell real products to people. Imagine skipping Amazon.com and buying something from a shop, maybe even your groceries to be delivered to your house, during a gaming session? And spending ATLAS you earned in game to do it.

Trading resources, selling loot, lending out assets, providing services and conveniences in game, etc. For example, someone might make a living operating their rescue ship getting paid by players that need the assistance. Or someone operating a taxi/Uber service on a CSS with their Lowbies. Or taking the Bitboat out for tours of the universe. The future of this virtual world will rely on people coming in and spending money - not just on those that are looking to withdraw value from it. Which is why I think the CSS's will be really attractive with their commercial centers. When mainstream real world brands set up shop and sell real products to people. Imagine skipping Amazon.com and buying something from a shop, maybe even your groceries to be delivered to your house, during a gaming session? And spending ATLAS you earned in game to do it.

content: So I listened to this and aside from feeling empathy for @Deleted User and the time he took which was respected as that was a LONG session. So many incredible things to take away and think about and I'm excited to see the direction things go but for one concern which I'll just mention. author: [AEP] Steve WoodyMUD
content:
So as I think feedback is important. I wanted to share some that might in someway help a little. (I totally appreciate I'm a small voice with a little budget compared to some, but I do think that I represent a group that the game needs to attract)

Before I invest in a project I always "dip my toe" just to see how things sit. I normally deploy 1% just to see what the process is and how things feel. After a week or so. I will investigate and then consider if I am deploying more. Either fully in or DCA. 

It's a strategy that has worked very well for me.

So I did that here. I deployed 1% to see what it was like. 

Going back to the earlier conversation about bots controlling the market liquidity. It's stopped me deploying anymore. Noone wants to invest and then see their investment -10% in less than 12 hours. Specially when you know it's been manipulated. Feeling that I'm not even buying from a playerbase but more just funding a project (which I was happy to do) but now because there are what I consider shady marketing tactics to min/max .... It just makes me question everything else and thus stop deploying.

Red flags like these can be enough these days to stop me investing altogether and whilst I appreciate it's only 100k ... 10 of me and you have 1mil. People like me add up and it's the above that caused me to dig deeper to really see what was happening with the order books.

I know there are thoughts and feelings around the bot situation but this goes back to my conversation about winning hearts and minds, specially when this space is so riddled with bad actors and exploiters. 

Again, disregard if needed. But I just wanted to share because I love the concept here and from what I have seen, the people also. I wont speak more on it and hope the feedback can be taken with the positive intention that it was intended.

author: defiantwyvern
content:
something about stacking crew for crafters. having a bunch might be good for low level material crafting, but only one crew will be able to work on a recipe at a time. If the high level recipes require expensive input materials, the capital cost of crew may be meaningless relative to the cost of operating a crafting business. You can't assign 50 crew to expedite making 1 of highest level upgrade material. Crank out low level materials? sure. but the high level crafting will likely be resource limited, not crew limited.

Also when NFT crew are added, I would guess that your airbike crew will start at the lowest level out of any crew. (If they do this, which to me would make sense to give better crew to start with the more expensive ships)

Once NFT crew get going, high level crafter NFT crew may become valuable/desirable, depending on the bonuses they afford and how difficult it is to level them up.

Not sure how crew rarity is determined, via source ship rarity during NFT split, RNG or whatever... Will C11 captain drop as Commander-class captain or just straight up captain? Probably TBD, given this is a ways out. 

What's near term is crew crafting and for that they are all the same.
